subject: combined-science

items.q: A question gives a mass of 250 g and a time of 2.0 minutes. Which pair of values should be substituted so that the working is in standard SI units?
items.correct: a mass of 0.25 kg and a time of 120 s
items.misconception: a mass of 250 g and a time of 2 minutes
items.why: Substitution is treated as copying digits, with the unit seen as a label added afterwards rather than part of the quantity. Convert to SI units first: grams to kilograms, centimetres to metres, minutes to seconds. The answer then comes out in the SI unit too.
items.random_wrong: a mass of 250 kg and a time of 120 s

items.q: In the first Appendix A list, what does HT in the left hand column tell you about an equation?
items.correct: Only Higher Tier papers can require that equation
items.misconception: Both tiers need it, but Higher Tier asks more often
items.why: The letters are read as a difficulty warning rather than as a tier label defining what each paper can ask. HT marks the tier: Foundation Tier papers cannot require an HT equation, Higher Tier papers can.
items.random_wrong: It is harder to rearrange than the equations near it

items.q: Which of these is the Appendix A equation for the weight of an object?
items.correct: weight = mass x gravitational field strength
items.misconception: weight = mass x acceleration of the object
items.why: W = m g and F = m a look identical, so g is read as an acceleration that must be happening now. g is the gravitational field strength. A stationary object still has weight m g.
items.random_wrong: weight = mass, because mass is the same as weight

items.q: A force of 12 N drags a crate 0.50 m along the line of action of the force. How much work is done?
items.correct: 6 J
items.why: 'Per' language from pressure and density is carried over to work, where nothing is divided. W = F s multiplies the force by the distance moved along the line of action of the force.

items.q: A spring of natural length 30 cm is stretched to 35 cm. The spring constant is 15 N/m. What force is applied to the spring?
items.why: 'Extension' is read as 'how long it is now' rather than 'how much longer it has become'. Extension is final length minus original length, converted to metres.

items.q: A cyclist travels at a steady 15 m/s for 4.0 s. What distance is travelled?
items.why: The equation is recalled as a triangle and the wrong pair is read off it. s = v t multiplies speed by time; dividing gives neither a distance nor sensible units.

items.q: A car speeds up from 4.0 m/s to 10 m/s in 8.0 s. What is its acceleration?
items.misconception: 1.3 m/s²
items.why: The equation is remembered as velocity over time, so the initial velocity is dropped. a = (∆v)/(t) uses the change in velocity: final minus initial.

items.q: A box is pushed with a force of 30 N while friction of 12 N acts backwards on it. Which force is used in F = m a?
items.correct: the resultant force, which is 18 N
items.misconception: the 30 N pushing force applied to the box
items.why: Questions often give several forces, and the first one quoted is taken as F. F = m a uses the resultant force, found by combining all the forces acting.
items.random_wrong: the 12 N force of friction on its own

items.q: A 1.0 kg mass moves at 4.0 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
items.correct: 8 J
items.why: The one half is treated as decoration and dropped when the sum is written out. E_k = 1/2 m v^2 includes the factor of one half.

items.q: A 2.0 kg bag is carried 5.0 m up a ramp and ends 3.0 m above its starting level. Taking g = 9.8 N/kg, what is the gain in gravitational potential energy?
items.why: The only length noticed is the one the object travelled along. h in E_p = m g h is the vertical height, not the distance along a slope.

items.q: An electric heater transfers 6000 J of energy in 30 s. Which statement about its power is correct?
items.correct: Its power is 200 W, from the energy over time
items.misconception: Its power is 180 000 W, from energy times time
items.why: Power is described as energy 'over time', which is read as energy across a period rather than a division. P = E/t divides the energy transferred by the time taken.
items.random_wrong: Its power is 0.005 W, from the time over the energy

items.q: A motor does 900 J of work in 45 s. What is its power output, and why?
items.correct: 20 W, because power is work done divided by time
items.misconception: 40 500 W, because power is work done times time
items.why: Power is described as energy 'over time', which is read as energy across a period rather than a division. P = E/t divides the energy transferred by the time taken.
items.random_wrong: 0.05 W, because power is time divided by work done

items.q: A motor is supplied with 500 J and usefully transfers 300 J, wasting 200 J. What is its efficiency?
items.correct: 0.6, from the useful 300 J divided by the 500 J input
items.misconception: 1.5, since a good motor can be more than 100% efficient
items.why: Efficiency is remembered as a score rather than as a fraction of the energy supplied. An answer above 1 means the fraction has been written upside down.
items.random_wrong: 0.4, from the wasted 200 J divided by the input

items.q: A pump has a total power input of 400 W and a useful power output of 250 W. What is its efficiency?
items.correct: 0.625, from the useful output divided by the total input
items.misconception: 1.6, from the total input divided by the useful output
items.why: The efficiency fraction is written down without checking which power belongs on top. efficiency = (useful power output)/(total power input); the answer can never be greater than 1.
items.random_wrong: 0.375, from the 150 W wasted power over the input

items.q: A wave has a frequency of 25 Hz and a wavelength of 400 cm. What is its wave speed?
items.why: Wavelengths are often drawn in centimetres on diagrams, so the unit is not questioned. Convert the wavelength to metres so the speed comes out in metres per second.

items.q: A current of 3.0 A flows for 2.0 minutes. What charge flows?
items.misconception: 6 C
items.why: The ampere is not recognised as a coulomb per second, so seconds are not required. Time must be in seconds, since one ampere is one coulomb per second.

items.q: A 6.0 V supply drives a current of 0.50 A through a resistor. What is its resistance?
items.why: The rearrangement is guessed because V = I R is only remembered in one form. Rearranging V = I R gives R = V/I, so divide the potential difference by the current.

items.q: A torch bulb works at 4.5 V and draws a current of 0.20 A. What is its power?
items.why: P = V I is confused with the many equations in this list that are fractions. P = V I is a product of the potential difference and the current.

items.q: A current of 3.0 A passes through a resistor of resistance 4.0 Ω. Which working gives the power dissipated?
items.correct: 3.0² x 4.0, giving 36 W
items.misconception: 3.0 x 4.0², which gives 48 W
items.why: The square is attached to the nearer symbol when the equation is written from memory. P = I^2 R squares the current, not the resistance.

items.q: A 2000 W heater is switched on for 5.0 minutes. How much energy is transferred?
items.why: Electricity bills use kilowatt-hours, so hours feel like an acceptable unit here. Standard SI units are required, so convert the time to seconds to get an answer in joules.

items.q: A charge of 8.0 C moves through a potential difference of 12 V. How much energy is transferred?
items.why: The equation is recalled as a fraction because so many electrical equations are fractions. E = Q V multiplies the charge flow by the potential difference.

items.q: A block of mass 240 kg has a volume of 0.30 m³. What is its density?
items.correct: 800 kg/m³
items.misconception: 72 kg/m³
items.why: Two quantities are given, so they are combined by multiplying, the more familiar operation. Density is mass per unit volume, so the mass is divided by the volume.

items.q: How should a student treat the twelve equations in the second Appendix A list?
items.correct: Select the right one from the equation sheet and apply it
items.misconception: Recall them from memory, as with the first list of equations
items.why: The two Appendix A lists look alike, so the difference between them is missed. The first list must be recalled; the second is printed on the sheet and must be selected and applied.
items.random_wrong: Memorise them as well, since none can be looked up

items.q: Which statement about the HT flags on the Physics equation sheet is correct?
items.correct: Higher Tier papers alone can require those equations
items.misconception: Every equation printed on the equation sheet is HT only
items.why: The sheet is seen as an extra for harder papers rather than as a resource for both tiers. Both tiers use the sheet. Only the equations marked HT are restricted to Higher Tier papers.
items.random_wrong: They mark the sheet equations that must also be recalled

items.q: A car accelerates uniformly from 5.0 m/s to 15 m/s over a distance of 50 m. Which working gives its acceleration?
items.why: The velocities are subtracted first because the bracket is read before the index. Each velocity is squared before subtracting: v^2 - u^2 is not (v - u)^2.

items.q: 0.50 kg of water is heated from 20 °C to 80 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. Which working gives the thermal energy transferred?
items.why: The final temperature is the number the question ends on, so it is the one remembered. ∆θ is the temperature change: final temperature minus starting temperature.

items.q: A sound wave has a frequency of 250 Hz. What is its period?
items.correct: 0.004 s, since period is 1 over the frequency
items.misconception: 250 s, because period and frequency match
items.why: Period and frequency are both described as timing the wave, so they are treated as one idea. They are reciprocals: a high frequency means a short period.
items.random_wrong: 500 s, since period is twice the frequency

items.q: How much energy is needed to melt 0.25 kg of ice at 0 °C? The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 334 000 J/kg.
items.why: The large printed number looks like the answer, so the mass is never used. The specific latent heat is the energy per kilogram, so it must be multiplied by the mass.

items.q: A sample has a volume of 500 cm³. What value should be substituted for V in ρ = m/V to give a density in kg/m³?
items.misconception: 500 m³
items.why: Converting a cubed unit needs division by 1000000, which is easy to forget. 1 m3 is 1000000 cm3, so divide by a million to reach standard SI units.

items.q: A time is given as 2.0 minutes. What is substituted?
items.correct: 120 s, because the SI unit of time is the second.
items.misconception: A time is a time, so 2.0 goes in whatever the unit says.
items.why: Time feels like a familiar everyday quantity, so the minute is not recognised as a non-SI unit needing conversion. Times must be converted to seconds before substitution; 2.0 minutes is 120 s.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A mass of 250 g is converted for use in W = m g. What is the risk?
items.correct: Writing 250 kg instead of 0.25 kg by changing the label and not the number.
items.misconception: Changing g to kg just means writing kg after the same number.
items.why: Unit conversion is remembered as a relabelling rule rather than a division or multiplication by 1000. Dividing by 1000 changes the number as well as the unit: 250 g becomes 0.25 kg.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is the weight of a 6.0 kg mass found on Earth?
items.correct: weight = mass x gravitational field strength, so W = 6.0 x 9.8 N.
items.misconception: The weight is 6.0 N because weight and mass are the same thing.
items.why: Everyday language uses 'weight' for what is measured in kilograms, so the two quantities are merged. Mass is in kilograms and does not change; weight is a force in newtons found from W = m g.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A distance is given as 50 cm in a work calculation. What is used?
items.correct: 0.50 m, converted to the SI unit of length.
items.misconception: The number 50 can go straight into W = F s.
items.why: The centimetre is so familiar that it is not registered as a non-SI unit. Convert centimetres to metres by dividing by 100 before substituting.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A spring constant is 15 N/m and the extension is 5.0 cm. What is the force?
items.correct: 0.75 N, using e = 0.05 m.
items.misconception: The force is 75 N, using the extension as 5.
items.why: Numbers are substituted in the units printed in the question rather than in metres. Convert the extension to metres first: 5.0 cm is 0.05 m, giving 0.75 N.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is a = (∆v)/(t) applied?
items.correct: The change in velocity is divided by the time taken.
items.misconception: The change in velocity is multiplied by the time taken.
items.why: Acceleration is loosely described as speed 'building up over time', which suggests multiplying. Acceleration is a rate, so the change in velocity is divided by the time it took.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is the momentum of a 2.0 kg trolley at 3.0 m/s found?
items.correct: 6.0 kg m/s, from momentum = mass x velocity.
items.misconception: 9.0 units, because the velocity is squared.
items.why: Momentum and kinetic energy both involve mass and velocity, so the squared term is carried across. p = m v has no square. Only kinetic energy squares the speed.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which quantity is squared in E_k = 1/2 m v^2?
items.correct: The speed only.
items.misconception: Kinetic energy is 1/2 x mass x speed, with the speed not squared.
items.why: The square is attached to the whole expression rather than to v alone. Only the speed is squared; doubling the mass doubles the kinetic energy but doubling the speed quadruples it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is gravitational potential energy calculated for a mass of 3.0 kg raised 2.0 m?
items.correct: 3.0 x 9.8 x 2.0, from E_p = m g h.
items.misconception: By multiplying weight by g by height.
items.why: Weight is already m g, but g is written in again from memory of the formula. Use mass x g x height, or equivalently weight x height. Using g twice doubles the answer wrongly.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the difference between energy transferred and power?
items.correct: Energy is measured in joules; power is the rate of transfer, in watts.
items.misconception: They are the same thing measured in different units.
items.why: Both are quoted for appliances, and joules and watts are used loosely in adverts. Power tells you how fast energy is transferred: one watt is one joule each second.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A machine does 900 J of work in 45 s. What is the power?
items.correct: 20 W, from power = (work done)/(time).
items.misconception: 0.05 W, from time divided by work done.
items.why: The fraction is inverted when the equation is written from memory. P = W/t puts the work done on top and the time underneath.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A motor is supplied with 500 J and usefully transfers 300 J. What is its efficiency?
items.correct: 0.6, from useful output divided by total input.
items.misconception: 1.67, from total input divided by useful output.
items.why: The larger number is instinctively placed on top so that the answer looks tidier. efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer), so the useful output goes on top.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A lamp wastes 80 J and usefully transfers 20 J from 100 J supplied. What is the efficiency?
items.correct: 0.2, using the 20 J usefully transferred.
items.misconception: 0.8, using the 80 J wasted.
items.why: The bigger energy figure is assumed to be the important one. Only the useful output energy transfer goes on top of the efficiency fraction.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 6.0 m. What is its speed?
items.correct: 300 m/s, from wave speed = frequency x wavelength.
items.misconception: 8.3 m/s, from frequency divided by wavelength.
items.why: Speed is associated with dividing, as in speed = distance over time. v = f λ multiplies the frequency by the wavelength.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A current of 3.0 A flows for 40 s. What charge flows?
items.correct: 120 C, from charge flow = current x time.
items.misconception: 0.075 C, from current divided by time.
items.why: Charge and current are both described in terms of flow, so the relationship is guessed. Q = I t multiplies the current by the time.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is the current found from V = I R?
items.correct: By dividing the potential difference by the resistance.
items.misconception: By multiplying the potential difference by the resistance.
items.why: Multiplication is the operation seen in the printed form of the equation, so it is repeated. I = V/R. A larger resistance gives a smaller current for the same potential difference.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A 2000 W heater runs for 300 s. What energy is transferred?
items.correct: 600000 J, from energy transferred = power x time.
items.misconception: 6.7 J, from power divided by time.
items.why: Energy and power are not clearly separated, so the operation is chosen at random. E = P t multiplies the power by the time in seconds.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A block of mass 240 kg has a volume of 0.30 m3. What is its density?
items.correct: 800 kg/m3, from density = (mass)/(volume).
items.misconception: 0.00125 kg/m3, from volume divided by mass.
items.why: The fraction is written down the wrong way when the equation is recalled quickly. ρ = m/V puts the mass on top and the volume underneath.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s a Higher Tier only equation?
items.correct: No, it is on the sheet without an HT flag, so both tiers may use it.
items.misconception: Anything with a square in it must be Higher Tier.
items.why: Difficulty of appearance is used as the test rather than the printed HT marking. The HT marking in the left hand column is the only thing that restricts an equation to Higher Tier.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is missing if v^2 - u^2 is set equal to a s?
items.correct: The factor of 2 on the right hand side.
items.misconception: Nothing; the 2 only applies when the object starts from rest.
items.why: The 2 looks like a detail and is dropped when the equation is copied from memory. The equation is v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s in all cases.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A mass in a ∆E = m c ∆θ calculation is given as 500 g. What is used?
items.misconception: 500, since specific heat capacity is per gram.
items.why: Specific heat capacity is quoted per kilogram, but the unit is not read carefully. Specific heat capacity is energy per kilogram per degree, so the mass must be in kilograms.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to the period when the frequency is doubled?
items.correct: It halves.
items.misconception: It doubles as well.
items.why: Both quantities describe how fast the wave oscillates, so they are assumed to change together. period = (1)/(frequency), so doubling the frequency halves the period.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A current of 3.0 A passes through a 4.0 ohm resistor. What power is dissipated?
items.correct: 36 W, because the current is squared first.
items.misconception: The current and the resistance are simply multiplied, giving 12 W.
items.why: P = I^2 R is remembered as a product, and the index on I is not noticed. The current must be squared before multiplying by the resistance.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is E = m L used when the mass is less than one kilogram?
items.correct: The latent heat is multiplied by the mass, giving a smaller energy.
items.misconception: The latent heat is divided by the mass, since the mass is small.
items.why: A mass below one seems to call for division so that the answer looks bigger. Multiplying by a mass less than one kilogram correctly gives less energy than L.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many cm³ make 1 m³, when converting a volume for use in ρ = m/V?
items.correct: 1 000 000, because 1 m = 100 cm so 1 m³ = 100 x 100 x 100 cm³. Divide a volume in cm³ by 1 000 000 to get m³.
items.misconception: There are 1000 cm³ in a cubic metre, so a volume in cm³ is converted to m³ by dividing by 1000.
items.why: Almost every conversion met before uses a factor of 1000: grams to kilograms, millilitres to litres, metres to kilometres. That familiar factor is applied to cm³ as well, and the need to cube the length factor of 100 is missed. Cubing the unit cubes the conversion factor. Since 1 m = 100 cm, 1 m³ = 100³ = 1 000 000 cm³. So 500 cm³ = 500 / 1 000 000 = 0.0005 m³, not 0.50 m³.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
